title: Learning speedups from random examples
formal: Does the low-end learning speedup hold using only independent uniform labeled examples? For each circuit family C specified below, suppose every polynomial-size subfamily has a randomized weak learner under the uniform distribution, with confidence \(1- 1/n\) and worst-case running time \(2^{n}/n^{\omega (1)}\). Must every polynomial-size subfamily then have, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) and \(a\ge 1, a\) randomized learner with error at most \(n^{- a}\), confidence at least \(1- 1/n\), and worst-case running time \(O(2^{n^{\varepsilon}})\), still using only independent uniform labeled examples?
context:
The source’s low-end theorem says that learning polynomial-size circuits slightly faster than their full truth-table scale already implies learning them in time \(2^{n^{\varepsilon}}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), with much better accuracy. Its theorem permits chosen membership queries.

The open-question paragraph asks about learning from random examples under the same uniform distribution. Here both sides use only independently sampled labeled points, so the faster learner cannot recover the missing power by choosing special inputs.

Pich’s 2025 Theorem 5.1 starts with nonuniform learning circuits supplied with random examples, but obtains a learner using nonadaptive membership queries. It is a related quantitative speedup, not the uniform random-example-to-random-example theorem stated here.
why: Tests whether the sharp gap in possible circuit-learning runtimes is a structural feature of passive learning, or relies on being able to choose labels to request. It connects the computational cost of statistical prediction with major circuit classes while keeping the distribution and available information fixed.
status_note: Read the conference model, low-end lemma and open-question passage, and the full preprint’s corresponding question. Read the later journal Theorem 5.1 and its access conventions. Searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a resolution of this precise passive low-end implication; they are not exhaustive and proofs were not independently audited.

references.title: Conspiracies Between Learning Algorithms, Circuit Lower Bounds, and Pseudorandomness
references.authors: Oliveira, Igor C. Carboni; Santhanam, Rahul
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 44; PDF page 44

definitions:
The unknown target is a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\). One example request supplies \((X,f(X))\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and independent of all earlier examples and the learner’s private random bits. The learner receives \(1^{n}\) and the fixed parameters specifying the target class. It may decide when to stop sampling, but cannot choose, correlate, condition or relabel the oracle’s next input. Reading and storing examples, internal computation and writing the hypothesis all count toward the time bound. A standard randomized multitape Turing machine with an example tape suffices; polynomial overheads in n do not alter the time classes used here. On every run it halts within the bound, including runs with labels outside the target promise. Its output is an explicitly encoded Boolean circuit h, with no example oracle or target-function gates. The hypothesis may belong to a larger circuit family than the target.

The error of h is \(\Pr_{X\text{ uniform}}[h(X)\ne f(X)]\). Confidence is the probability, jointly over the sample and internal randomness, of obtaining a hypothesis satisfying the stated error bound, for every eligible f and every sufficiently large n. A weak learner has error at most \(1/2- n^{- b}\) for some fixed \(b\ge 1\). The exponent b and the learner may depend on the fixed target subfamily. A strong learner here means that for each fixed \(a\ge 1\) there is an algorithm attaining error \(n^{- a}\); this is not a claim of polynomial dependence on a variable accuracy input.

The circuit families are \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}, \mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\) for a fixed prime \(p, \mathrm{ACC}^{0}, \mathrm{TC}^{0}, \mathrm{NC}^{1}\), Boolean formulas, and unrestricted Boolean circuits. Circuits have input bits and Boolean constants, and size is the number of wires. \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) uses \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) gates of unbounded fan-in and NOT gates; \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\) also permits gates testing whether the number of true inputs is 0 modulo p. \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) permits such modular gates for fixed moduli, with the choice of moduli independent of n. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) additionally permits unweighted majority gates, outputting 1 when at least half their inputs are 1. For these four families a subfamily fixes both a constant depth bound d and a size bound \(n^{k}\), where \(k\ge 1\) is constant; modular parameters are also fixed. Boolean formulas use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) and NOT, have fan-out one except for input variables, and at most \(n^{k}\) wires. Unrestricted Boolean circuits use those same gate types, allow shared subcircuits and have at most \(n^{k}\) wires. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) uses bounded fan-in Boolean gates, polynomial size and depth at most \(d \log _{2}(n+2)\) for fixed d. Taking all fixed k,d covers the source’s polynomial-size \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) convention. Every circuit description is finite, with gate types and wire endpoints in binary.

For each fixed family C, the premise quantifies over ALL its fixed polynomial-size subfamilies: for each k and any fixed depth/modular parameters, there exist b, a uniform learner A and a time bound \(T_{A}(n)\) such that for every constant \(M>0, T_{A}(n)\le 2^{n}/n^{M}\) for all sufficiently large n. Thus \(2^{n}/n^{\omega (1)}\) means a superpolynomial saving, not just \(2^{n}/n^{10}\) and not a different algorithm for each M. The conclusion quantifies over every target subfamily and every fixed \(\varepsilon >0,a\ge 1\); the algorithm and the hidden constant may depend on these fixed choices, but not on n or f. There is no requirement that one algorithm accept descriptions of arbitrary target families. Learners are uniform algorithms across input lengths; the target circuits themselves need not be uniformly generated. The implication is unconditional and applies separately to each listed family.

This card makes explicit the low-end, polynomial-target branch of conference Lemma 24. The source also has a high-end branch relating learning subexponential-size targets to quasipolynomial-time learning of polynomial-size targets. The generic extracted question referred to that lemma as a whole; the present target selects its main low-end branch rather than asserting that this one implication is equivalent to both branches together.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the stated implication for the listed circuit families, with only independent uniform labeled examples in both the premise and conclusion. A positive result must supply the all-\(\varepsilon\), all-fixed-accuracy speedup whenever the weak-learning premise holds. A negative result must establish failure of that implication for an eligible family; a lower bound in a restricted learning model, or an algorithm that needs membership queries, does not by itself refute or establish it. The separate high-end branch is not required by this card.
